Looking For A New Year's Resolution? Start Thinking Long-Term.
Amir Husain, Forbes, 2022-12-29

I am not one of those guys sitting in a chair on the front veranda, yelling at children to get off the lawn. I promise. But it is hard not to agree that we are fast becoming a society with comically short attention spans. If nothing else, this is evidenced by the popularity of ubiquitous social networks that offer short bursts of content, full of dopamine hits but often absent real meaning. Focusing on instant gratification and enjoyment in the present moment means that building value over the long term, being patient, and working hard for a long time to achieve something genuinely worth achieving are no longer seen as fashionable or desirable. The shorter the message, the better. A tweet is preferred over an essay, which is preferred over a book. A pause in speech makes us uncomfortable. A TikTok clip is better than a film. Job hopping every few months is just the new normal. We tire of everything so quickly.

All of the outstanding achievements of the human race have required years, decades, and generations of effort. When you visit the Duomo in Milan or the Sagrada Familia in Barcelona, you are reminded that these buildings took centuries to complete. No one involved in the design and initial construction survived to see the end. They considered it worth their while because the end goal even one achieved beyond their lifetimes - deserved dedication and hard work.

If we are to build a future that is truly meaningful, we cannot forget how greatness is achieved: by committing oneself to a goal over the long haul. Delayed gratification needs to be once again normalized and celebrated.

The statistics support this argument. According to a paper published by Daniel Romer of the University of Pennsylvania, teenagers who are able to delay gratification have been shown to have better control over risk-taking tendencies, such as drug use. Delayed gratification leads to better mental and physical health, higher education and income levels, and better social skills. In contrast, those who prioritize immediate gratification have been found to fall prey to tendencies that can ruin lives.

Shonna Waters, a Ph.D. in Industrial-Organizational Psychology from the University of Minnesota, explains that individuals who can delay gratification are more likely to succeed in their careers and achieve their goals. She attributes improved career success, improved self-worth, and better health to an ability to delay gratification.

For example, countries with high levels of long-term orientation, such as Japan and South Korea, have experienced rapid economic growth and development. In contrast, countries focusing on shortterm gratification have struggled with economic and social problems.

Creating a culture that values long-term achievement and dedication helps shift the focus back toward delayed gratification.

Yuko Munakata, a psychologist at the University of California, explains the results of a “patience” test involving children and their ability to delay the gratification of eating a marshmallow: “On average, the Japanese kids waited the maximum 15 minutes, sitting by themselves. The American kids, on average, ate the marshmallow within three or four minutes.” She writes, “An intriguing thing we found is that, where there were these cultural routines around waiting, what predicted whether or not kids waited was not their self-control abilities, but their sensitivity to social conventions. That can support delaying gratification in the classic marshmallow task and things like success in relationships and school.”

Children care about cultural cues and the social norms that surround them. A societal shift toward delayed gratification starts with questioning our behavior and family traditions. Teaching children the value of delayed gratification and the importance of setting long-term goals can help to create a mindset that prioritizes hard work and planning over instant satisfaction.

Any student of history will confirm that lasting greatness is achieved through years, decades, and even generations of labor and dedication. If we want to build a future that is genuinely beneficial and meaningful, it is high time we start to prioritize long-term thinking and emphasize the value of delayed gratification.

We can start with ourselves.
